title: How a Latin sentence works

objectives.can: Find the verb, its subject and its object in a short Latin sentence by their endings, not their position.

explanation.summary: A Latin sentence is held together by endings, not by word order. The ending of a verb says who acts; the ending of a noun says whether it is the subject or the object. Once you read endings, you can read Latin in the order the author wrote it.

sections.heading: The verb carries its subject
body: In English a verb needs a separate subject: 'he saw', 'we saw'. In Latin the ending of the verb already says who acts. *Vidit* means 'he (or she, or it) saw'; *vidimus* means 'we saw'. No separate word for 'he' or 'we' is needed, and none is usually written. When a Latin sentence does name a subject, it is a noun in the nominative case, such as *Deus* in *vidit Deus*, 'God saw'.

A finite verb therefore has two jobs at once: it names the action and it names the person who does it. The table sets out the six endings. Do not learn them as a list yet; later lessons teach each tense. For now learn to notice them.
The word for 'is' and 'was' is the verb *sum*. Its forms (*est*, *sunt*, *erat*) are verbs like any other and contain their subject in the same way.

sections.heading: The noun shows its job by its ending
body: A noun that is the subject of a verb stands in the nominative case; a noun that is the object stands in the accusative. The two are told apart by their endings. In *vidit Deus lucem*, 'God saw the light', *Deus* is the subject and *lucem* the object, and the ending -em of *lucem* is what shows it, not the fact that *lucem* stands after the verb.

This is why the sentence could be reordered without changing who does what. The next lessons teach the endings of each case. Here, notice that accusative singular endings very often end in -m (*lucem*, *viam*, *terram*, *Jesum*).

sections.heading: Where the verb stands
body: Word order in Latin is free but not random. In the classical prose of the Roman historians the verb often comes last: the order subject, object, verb. In the Vulgate the verb often comes early, as in *creavit Deus cælum et terram*, because the translation follows the order of the Hebrew or Greek it renders. Neither order is a rule. Read the endings first, and let the order tell you what the writer stressed.
There are no words for 'the' and 'a'. A noun such as *homo* may be 'a man' or 'the man'; the context and the English alongside the Latin help you decide.

sections.heading: Small words that join and negate
body: *Et* means 'and', and so does *-que*, which attaches to the end of the word it joins: *Dixitque Deus* means 'And God said'. *Sed* means 'but'. *Non* negates the verb and normally stands just before it: *non comprehenderunt*, 'they did not grasp'. These words are not nouns or verbs and have no case or person; you recognise them by sight.

misunderstandings: Do not read Latin in the order of English. The first noun is not always the subject, and the noun just after the verb is not always the object. Check the endings.
Do not look for a missing pronoun. A Latin verb with no stated subject is complete: *vidit* is a whole clause, 'he saw'.
A subject pronoun, when it is written, is a signal of emphasis or contrast, not a grammatical need. The pronoun *ego* in *ego baptizo* ('I baptize') stresses 'I' against another person.
The final -s of a verb (*es*) means 'you', but the final -s of a noun is often a plural or a case ending. Verbs and nouns have different endings; do not mix them.

deeper.heading: Why the Vulgate puts the verb early
body: Jerome's Latin translation of the Old Testament follows the Hebrew closely, and Hebrew narrative regularly opens a clause with its verb. The Latin New Testament follows the Greek, which likewise often puts the verb early. A Latin writer of the same period who was not translating would more often have placed the verb at the end. This is one reason the order of a Vulgate sentence cannot be read as the order of the Latin of Cicero or Caesar.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: In the beginning God created heaven, and earth.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

examples.analysis: The verb *creavit* comes first and contains its subject, 'he created'. The nominative noun *Deus* names who: God is the subject. *terram* (like *cælum*) ends in -m: they are the objects, 'heaven and earth'. The order is verb, subject, object, as in the Hebrew.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And God saw the light that it was good; and he divided the light from the darkness.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

examples.analysis: *vidit* is 'he saw', with its subject in the ending; *Deus* is that subject named. *lucem*, 'the light', is the object. The ending -em, the accusative of *lux*, shows it, not the fact that *lucem* follows the verb.

quoted.title: John
quoted.english: He was in the world, and the world was made by him, and the world knew him not.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

examples.analysis: Here the verb comes last: *mundus eum non cognovit*. *mundus* is the subject, *eum* the object ('him'), *non* negates the verb, and *cognovit* ends the clause, 'the world did not know him'. This is the order of classical prose, subject, object, verb.

quoted.title: John
quoted.english: And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we saw his glory, the glory as it were of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

examples.analysis: *vidimus* means 'we saw'. The ending -mus contains the subject, so no word for 'we' is written. *gloriam* ('glory') is the object, an accusative in -m.

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: For the Lord knoweth the way of the just: and the way of the wicked shall perish.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

examples.analysis: *novit Dominus viam* is verb, subject, object: 'the Lord knows the way'. *Dominus* is the nominative; *viam* is the accusative, as its -m ending shows. If the order were reversed, so that viam came first, the sense would not change.

options: It writes the article as an ending on the noun
It leaves them out only in poetry
It has neither: context decides between 'a man' and 'the man'
practice.explain: Latin has no articles. *homo* alone may be 'a man' or 'the man', and the translator chooses. The edition's English has 'a man' here.

check.prompt: What does the -que of *Dixitque Deus* do?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And God said: Be light made. And light was made.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

options: It makes the sentence a question
It joins the clause to the previous one, 'and'
It marks the verb as past
check.explain: *-que* means 'and' and is written on the end of the word it follows. *Dixit* is past by its own ending; -que does not mark the past.

check.prompt: What does *sed* do in *Non erat ille lux, sed ut testimonium perhiberet*?

quoted.title: John
quoted.english: He was not the light, but was to give testimony of the light.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

options: It marks a contrast with what came before: 'but'
It adds a second reason: 'and also'
check.explain: *sed* means 'but'. Here it follows a negative clause and sets a contrast with it: he was not the light, but was to bear witness.

check.prompt: Which statement about a Latin clause such as *vidit Deus lucem* is correct?
options: The first noun is always the subject
A subject must be written as a separate word
The endings, not the position, show which noun is subject and which is object
check.explain: The nominative marks the subject, the accusative the object. Neither order nor position decides, and the ending of the verb can itself supply the subject.

reading.why: Five verses made of short clauses in which the verb and its subject are easy to find: *creavit Deus*, *vidit Deus*, *Dixitque Deus*. Find the verb of each clause first, then its subject, then its object.
